Shooters
SHOO-terz
n. pl. (archers; those who shoot from a wall or a bow)
From shoot, Saxon sceotan, to dart or let fly. In 2 Samuel 11:24 it renders a Hebrew participle of yarah, to shoot or cast.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Joab's messenger reports from Rabbah: “And the shooters shot from off the wall upon thy servants; and some of the king's servants be dead, and thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also” (2 Samuel 11:24). The sentence is constructed to bury one name in a casualty list, and David knows it, because David wrote the order. The archers on the wall were real, the losses were real, and the whole arrangement was a murder dressed as a battle report. David's answer is the most chilling line in the chapter: “Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another” (2 Samuel 11:25). He blames the sword. He consoles the general. He takes the widow. The Authorized Version prints shooters here, where the margin of 1 Samuel 31:3 also offers it for the archers who wounded Saul. The dictionary notes the grim symmetry: the shooters on the wall at Rabbah served a king's adultery, and the shooters at Gilboa ended a king's reign. Psalm 51 is the only honest sequel to this verse, and it is David's.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): SHOOTER, noun One that shoots; an archer; a gunner.

expand to see more

SHOOTER, noun One that shoots; an archer; a gunner.

SHOOT, verb transitive To let fly and drive with force; as, to shoot an arrow.

2. To discharge and cause to be driven with violence; as, to shoot a ball.

3. To send out; to push forth; as, a plant shoots a branch.

SHOOT, verb intransitive To be emitted, sent or driven along.

Key Scripture

2Sa 11:24 — "And the shooters shot from off the wall upon thy servants; and some of the king's servants be dead, and thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."

2Sa 11:25 — "Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another: make thy battle more strong against the city, and overthrow it: and encourage thou him."

Psa 51:4 — "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest."

Modern Corruption

David's sin is often handled as a lapse or a failure of leadership; Scripture calls it murder and adultery, confessed as such.

expand to see more

Two corruptions meet here. The first excuses David by his office or his era — a king's prerogative, an ancient custom, a moment of weakness. Scripture records a conspiracy to kill a faithful soldier so the king could keep the soldier's wife, and Nathan names it plainly: thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword.

The second corruption is despair — the assumption that such a man is beyond grace. Psalm 51 refuses both. David calls it evil in God's sight, pleads nothing but mercy, and is forgiven without the sin being minimised. That is the Reformed doctrine of repentance in one psalm.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Saxon sceotan, to let fly; renders a participle of Hebrew yarah, to shoot, at 2 Samuel 11:24.

expand to see more

Saxon sceotan, to dart, to let fly.

Hebrew yarah, to shoot, cast, or throw.

2 Samuel 11:24 is the only place the Authorized Version prints shooters in the text.

The margin of 1 Samuel 31:3 offers the shooters, men with bows, for the archers at Gilboa.

The casualty report was written to conceal the murder of Uriah.

Usage

"the shooters shot from off the wall"

"thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also"

"the sword devoureth one as well as another"
